# The whole shebang

::: {.chapter-goals}
**By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:**

- distinguish a bioinformatics tool from a script and a workflow;
- explain the separate jobs of modules, Conda, containers, Nextflow and SLURM;
- distinguish Docker/OCI image building from Singularity/Apptainer execution;
- explain where Git, GitHub and CI/CD fit into scientific software development;
- trace one sequencing sample through the complete engineering stack; and
- recognize claims that a reproducible workflow can—and cannot—support.
:::

## Why a biologist should care

Imagine that you receive paired-end sequencing reads and answer a biological
question with four programs. You record the commands in a notebook. Six months
later, one program has changed, a library is missing and the commands run in the
wrong order on a new computer. A collaborator cannot reproduce the result. On
an HPC cluster, the same commands compete for memory or accidentally run on the
login node.

The biological logic may have been correct. The engineering around it was not
strong enough to preserve and communicate that logic.

Modern bioinformatics therefore has two inseparable responsibilities:

1. **Analytical responsibility:** choose methods that are appropriate for the
   biological question and interpret their outputs correctly.
2. **Engineering responsibility:** make the inputs, software, execution,
   decisions and outputs traceable, testable and repeatable.

This book concentrates on the second responsibility without pretending it can
replace the first. A beautifully engineered workflow can still run an
inappropriate aligner. A biologically appropriate analysis can still be
unreproducible if its software and execution are undocumented. Industry teams
need both kinds of judgment.

## Engineering objective

Before installing or coding anything, we need a map of the system. You should
be able to point to each layer and answer:

- What problem does this layer solve?
- What information enters and leaves it?
- Which other layer does it depend on?
- What evidence tells us that it behaved as intended?

If these layers are blurred together, troubleshooting becomes guesswork. For
example, changing a Conda package cannot fix a SLURM account error, and changing
a Nextflow channel cannot repair a corrupt FASTQ file.

## Start with files and transformations

Most command-line bioinformatics programs behave like transformations:

```text
input files + parameters + software → output files + logs
```

In our teaching project:

- **FastQC** reads FASTQ files and writes quality reports.
- **Trim Galore** reads paired FASTQ files and writes trimmed paired FASTQ
  files plus reports.
- **Bowtie2** reads trimmed FASTQ files and a reference index, then writes SAM
  alignment records.
- **SAMtools** sorts, indexes and validates the alignments in BAM format.

Each program is a **tool**. A tool normally performs one focused operation.
Connecting the tools creates a **pipeline**.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "The analytical path used throughout the book. Trimming creates two branches: post-trim quality control and alignment."
flowchart LR
    R["Paired FASTQ"] --> Q1["Raw FastQC"]
    R --> T["Trim Galore"]
    T --> Q2["Post-trim FastQC"]
    T --> A["Bowtie2"]
    X["Reference index"] --> A
    A --> S["SAMtools sort"]
    S --> V["BAM validation"]
```

Notice that this is not simply a list. Raw FastQC and trimming can begin from
the same input. Post-trim FastQC and alignment must wait for trimming. Alignment
also needs the reference index. These dependencies form a directed graph.

## Tool, command, script, pipeline and workflow

These words are related but not interchangeable.

| Term | Meaning in this book | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Tool** | A program that performs a focused operation | `samtools` |
| **Command** | One request to run a program with particular arguments | `samtools quickcheck sample.bam` |
| **Script** | A saved text file containing commands and control logic | `run_manual.sh` |
| **Pipeline** | The connected analytical steps from input to result | FASTQ → trim → align → BAM |
| **Workflow** | An executable model of tasks, dependencies, inputs, outputs and resources | `main.nf` |
| **Workflow run** | One execution of a workflow with specific inputs, settings and software | the five-task chr22 run |

A Bash script can implement a pipeline. A workflow engine adds explicit task
contracts, dependency scheduling, isolated work directories, caching,
resource requests and alternative execution backends. That does not make Bash
obsolete: every Nextflow process in this book ultimately runs shell commands.

## The complete stack

Our analytical graph sits inside a larger engineering system.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "The layers are complementary. Nextflow coordinates commands supplied by an environment or image and launches tasks through an executor."
flowchart TB
    BQ["Biological question"] --> DATA["Input data + metadata"]
    DATA --> WF["Nextflow workflow logic"]
    SW["Software layer<br/>Conda environment or OCI image"] --> WF
    CFG["Parameters + configuration"] --> WF
    WF --> EX["Executor<br/>local or SLURM"]
    EX --> RT["Task runtime<br/>host, Conda or Singularity"]
    RT --> OUT["Outputs + logs + reports"]
    OUT --> QC["Technical and biological review"]
    GIT["Git + GitHub<br/>history and collaboration"] -. records .-> WF
    GIT -. records .-> CFG
    CI["CI/CD automation"] -. checks and publishes .-> GIT
```

The arrows do not mean that Git executes FastQC or that SLURM installs
SAMtools. Each layer has a narrower responsibility.

## The host operating system

The **host** is the computer or compute node on which a process ultimately
runs. It supplies the kernel, processors, memory, filesystems and security
controls. On a laptop you may administer much of the host. On an institutional
cluster, platform administrators control it.

This matters because neither Conda nor a container creates CPUs or memory.
Containers also share the host kernel; they are not complete virtual machines.
Architecture and operating-system compatibility still matter.

**Question answered by the host:** *What machine resources and operating-system
services exist?*

## Cluster modules

An HPC **module system** lets administrators offer multiple versions of
cluster-provided software. Loading a module commonly modifies environment
variables such as `PATH`, which controls where the shell searches for
executables.

Examples might include Java, Singularity or a compiler. Module names and
versions are local to the cluster.

**Question answered by modules:** *Which administrator-provided software should
this shell session see?*

Modules are not Conda environments. A module may expose the Java needed to
start Nextflow while a Conda environment supplies FastQC and SAMtools. Because
both can modify `PATH`, they can also conflict. Later we will inspect the active
layers rather than assuming which executable is being used.

## Conda environments and channels

**Conda** is a package and environment manager. A Conda environment is an
isolated directory containing selected programs and their dependencies. For
example, SAMtools depends on libraries for compressed genomic file formats.
Conda attempts to choose a compatible set.

A **channel** is a package repository. It is a source from which Conda obtains
package metadata and package files. Bioconda distributes many bioinformatics
packages; conda-forge distributes a broad range of supporting software and
libraries. Channel order and priority affect which builds the solver may
select.

**Question answered by Conda:** *Which package versions and compatible
libraries are installed in this environment?*

Conda improves control over software, but an environment specification alone
does not freeze the host kernel, scheduler, external reference data or every
future package build. Reproducibility has multiple layers.

## OCI images, Docker and containers

An **OCI image** is a packaged, read-only filesystem plus metadata describing
how software should run. OCI refers to open container standards. **Docker** is
one widely used platform for building and running OCI-compatible images.

A **container** is a running process created from an image. The distinction is
similar to a class recipe versus one instantiated object, or a cake recipe
versus one baked cake—although every analogy has limits.

An image can contain the Conda-resolved tools, their libraries and selected
operating-system files. A registry such as GitHub Container Registry stores and
distributes images.

| Concept | Mutable while building/running? | Role |
|---|---:|---|
| Dockerfile | Yes, it is source text | Recipe for building an image |
| Image | Normally treated as immutable | Packaged filesystem and metadata |
| Tag | Can be moved to another image | Human-friendly name such as `v0.1.0` |
| Digest | Identifies exact image content | Immutable content address |
| Container | Has a writable runtime layer | A process running from an image |
| Registry | Stores and distributes images | GHCR, Docker Hub or another service |

**Question answered by an image:** *What packaged userspace and tools should
travel with this task?*

::: {.callout-warning title="A tag is not an immutable identity"}
The label `latest` can point to different image content tomorrow. A digest
identifies exact content. Friendly tags are useful for humans; digests are
stronger evidence for an exact runtime.
:::

## Singularity and Apptainer on HPC

Docker normally relies on a long-running privileged service called a daemon.
Multi-user HPC centers commonly do not allow users to run that service. They
often provide **Singularity** or **Apptainer**, which can execute container
images using an HPC-oriented security and filesystem model.

Singularity can pull an OCI image and create a **SIF**—a Singularity Image
Format file. Nextflow can then execute individual tasks inside that SIF while
SLURM assigns the compute node.

Docker and Singularity therefore are not two words for the same operation in
our project:

- GitHub Actions uses a Docker-oriented build process to create the OCI image.
- DLDCC uses Singularity to run the resulting image as a SIF.

**Question answered by Singularity:** *How should this HPC task enter and run
the packaged container environment?*

## Nextflow: dependency and task orchestration

**Nextflow** is a workflow engine. We describe processes with input and output
contracts. Channels carry values—such as sample identifiers and file paths—to
processes. When all required inputs are available, Nextflow creates a task.

Nextflow can:

- stage task inputs into an isolated work directory;
- launch ready tasks without waiting unnecessarily for unrelated tasks;
- request CPUs, memory and time;
- run a task with Conda or inside a container;
- submit tasks locally, to SLURM or to other executors;
- record logs, traces, timelines and reports; and
- reuse a matching successful task with `-resume`.

Nextflow does not decide whether Bowtie2 is biologically appropriate. It also
does not replace Bowtie2: it coordinates the command that runs Bowtie2.

**Question answered by Nextflow:** *Which task is ready, what are its inputs and
outputs, what resources/runtime does it require, and can prior work be reused?*

## Executors and SLURM

An **executor** is the Nextflow component that decides how tasks are launched.
With the local executor, tasks run on the current machine. With the SLURM
executor, Nextflow writes job wrappers and submits them to the cluster
scheduler.

**SLURM** is a workload manager. It places jobs on shared compute resources
according to requested CPUs, memory, time, partition, account and site policy.
It tracks queued, running, completed and failed jobs.

SLURM does not understand that trimming must precede alignment. Nextflow knows
the data dependency and submits the alignment task only when its inputs exist.
Nextflow does not decide which physical node is free. SLURM does.

**Question answered by the executor and scheduler:** *How, where and when
should this ready task run?*

## Git and GitHub: traceable change and collaboration

**Git** records snapshots of selected files and the relationships between those
snapshots. It lets a team inspect what changed, why it changed and which exact
revision was used. Branches allow work to be reviewed before it becomes part of
the main history. Tags can name releases.

**GitHub** hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration services such as
issues, pull requests, reviews, releases and automation.

Git should track source and small evidence artifacts:

- Nextflow and Bash source;
- environment specifications;
- Dockerfiles;
- configuration without secrets;
- tests and documentation; and
- small reports needed to support claims.

Git is generally a poor home for large FASTQ, BAM, index, cache and container
files. Sensitive data must never be placed in a public repository.

**Question answered by Git:** *Which source revision and documented decisions
produced this project state?*

## CI/CD: automated feedback and delivery

**Continuous integration (CI)** means automatically integrating and checking
small changes frequently. A CI workflow may lint files, render documentation,
run a small test and verify that a container contains required tools.

**Continuous delivery** means keeping a tested artifact ready to release or
publishing it through a controlled process. **Continuous deployment** goes
further: a passing change is automatically deployed to its target environment.

In our work:

- GitHub Actions building and smoke-checking an image is CI plus artifact
  delivery.
- GitHub Actions publishing this Quarto book to GitHub Pages is automated
  deployment of documentation.
- Running a research pipeline on new samples is not automatically “CI/CD.” It
  is a workflow execution and may require separate authorization, review and
  data controls.

Automation supplies evidence; it does not create scientific truth. A green
check means the configured checks passed—not that every biological or clinical
requirement has been validated.

**Question answered by CI/CD:** *Which checks and publication actions should
happen automatically when source changes or a release is created?*

## Trace one sample through the stack

Consider the sample identifier `sim_chr22`.

1. Two FASTQ files and sample metadata describe the input.
2. Git identifies the exact workflow, configuration, environment and container
   recipe revision.
3. Nextflow creates the raw-QC and trimming tasks because both can consume the
   original read pair.
4. The selected profile tells Nextflow to use the local or SLURM executor and a
   Conda environment or Singularity image.
5. On DLDCC, Nextflow submits a job wrapper to SLURM.
6. SLURM assigns a compute node with the requested resources.
7. Singularity starts the task inside the project SIF and makes required host
   paths visible through bind mounts.
8. FastQC or Trim Galore runs with the inputs staged by Nextflow.
9. The task writes output and logs in its isolated work directory.
10. Nextflow records task status, publishes selected results and enables cache
    reuse.
11. Technical checks confirm that files exist, are readable and have expected
    summaries.
12. A qualified analyst still decides whether the results are biologically
    meaningful for the intended use.

No single technology performs all twelve responsibilities.

## Three kinds of reproducibility

The word *reproducible* is often used too broadly. In this book we separate:

1. **Computational repeatability:** rerunning the same inputs, code, parameters
   and runtime produces acceptably equivalent outputs.
2. **Computational reproducibility:** another person can reconstruct the
   analysis from recorded source, software, data provenance and instructions.
3. **Scientific reproducibility:** independent evidence supports the same
   scientific conclusion.

This project primarily demonstrates the first two on a small synthetic test
fixture. It does not demonstrate clinical validation or independent scientific
replication.

::: {.callout-important title="Engineering evidence has a scope"}
A successful Nextflow run proves that configured tasks completed. A valid BAM
proves that the file passes selected structural checks. A container digest
identifies image content. None of these facts alone proves that a method is
appropriate for diagnosis, that a biological conclusion is correct or that the
workflow is production-ready.
:::

## Common misconceptions

### “Conda and Docker do the same thing”

Both help control software, but at different boundaries. Conda manages packages
inside an environment. An OCI image packages a broader userspace and metadata.
We will use Conda to resolve tools and then package that environment in an
image.

### “Nextflow runs the cluster”

Nextflow models and submits work. SLURM manages shared cluster resources. The
Nextflow SLURM executor connects the two.

### “The container includes my input data”

Our image contains software, not the large analysis inputs. At runtime, files
are normally mounted or staged into the container.

### “If CI is green, the pipeline is validated”

CI reports only the checks we encoded. Validation requires defined intended
use, requirements, acceptance criteria, evidence and—where applicable—formal
quality or regulatory processes.

### “GitHub is Git”

Git is the version-control system. GitHub is a hosting and collaboration
platform built around Git repositories. Git works without GitHub.

Without looking back, complete the final column.

| Layer | Primary responsibility | Your one-sentence explanation |
|---|---|---|
| Bioinformatics tool | Perform one analytical operation | |
| Module system | Expose administrator-provided cluster software | |
| Conda | Resolve and install package environments | |
| OCI image | Package software and userspace | |
| Singularity | Execute the packaged environment on HPC | |
| Nextflow | Coordinate tasks and data dependencies | |
| SLURM | Schedule jobs and allocate cluster resources | |
| Git/GitHub | Record, share and review source changes | |
| CI/CD | Automatically check and deliver defined artifacts | |

Save this table in your learning notes. At the end of the book, revise each
sentence using the evidence you created.

## Verification checkpoint

Match each scenario to its **primary** layer. Some scenarios involve several
layers; choose the one that owns the stated decision.

1. SAMtools 1.19.2 and its libraries must be installed together.
2. Trimming must finish before alignment begins.
3. Five ready tasks are waiting for available compute nodes.
4. An HPC task must enter the project SIF before running FastQC.
5. A reviewer wants to inspect the exact source change that introduced a new
   parameter.
6. A pushed pull request should automatically render the documentation and run
   a smoke test.
7. A collaborator wants the exact image content rather than whatever `latest`
   means today.
8. An analyst must decide whether Bowtie2 is appropriate for bisulfite-treated
   reads.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show the answers"}
1. Conda/package environment.
2. Nextflow workflow dependency.
3. SLURM scheduler.
4. Singularity/Apptainer runtime.
5. Git history and GitHub review.
6. CI automation.
7. OCI image digest.
8. Biological/methodological judgment—not the workflow engine.
:::

You are ready to continue when you can explain *why* each answer is different,
not merely recite the product names.

## Try it yourself

Draw the stack for one analysis you already know. It can be an R script, a
microscopy workflow or a sequencing analysis. Identify:

- input data;
- analytical tools;
- software environment;
- ordering/dependencies;
- execution location;
- outputs and logs;
- version-control evidence; and
- acceptance criteria.

If a layer is absent, write “not yet controlled” rather than inventing it. That
gap is useful information.

## What to remember

- Biological validity and engineering reproducibility support one another but
  are not the same claim.
- A tool performs an operation; a workflow engine coordinates operations and
  their dependencies.
- Modules, Conda, containers, Nextflow and SLURM solve different problems and
  can be used together.
- Docker/OCI builds and distributes the image; Singularity/Apptainer executes
  that packaged environment on our HPC system.
- Git records source history; GitHub supports collaboration; CI/CD automates
  explicitly defined checks and delivery.
- Every green check, checksum and report has a limited meaning. Good engineers
  state that meaning accurately.
